blocks.text: An API key is about as simple as authentication gets, a single string that a client attaches to every request, and the server trusts whoever holds it.
That simplicity is exactly why API keys are everywhere, they need no login flow, no redirect, no session negotiation, just a value copied into a header.

That same simplicity is also why they are so easy to get wrong, a key is just a piece of text, and any piece of text that leaks, gets logged, or gets committed to a repository is a piece of text anyone can now use as if they were you.
1. What an API Key Actually Is

blocks.alt: What an API Key Actually Is
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440373675-796935657.png

An API key is nothing more than a long, hard to guess string that a server generates and hands to a client, and that the client then sends back with every subsequent request as proof of identity. There is no cryptography happening on the client's side, no signature to compute, the entire mechanism relies on the string itself being secret and being checked against a record the server keeps.

Because the key alone is proof, whoever has a copy of it can act as the party it was issued to, no additional check confirms that the sender is the original recipient. This is the central tradeoff of API keys, they are trivially simple to implement and use, and that simplicity comes directly at the cost of having no built in way to tell a legitimate holder from someone who merely copied the string.

blocks.title: A key is a bearer secret
blocks.content: Whoever presents a valid API key is treated as though they are the party it was issued to, there is no second factor confirming that.

blocks.title: A simple mental model
blocks.content: An API key is a bit like a physical key to a specific door, whoever holds it can open that door, which is exactly why losing track of a copy is so risky.

blocks.text: 2. Generating Keys That Are Actually Hard to Guess

A good API key needs enough randomness that guessing it is computationally hopeless, which means using a cryptographically secure random source rather than anything predictable like a counter, a timestamp, or a hash of the user's email. Most languages provide a secrets or crypto module specifically built for this purpose, and reaching for it instead of a general purpose random function matters more than it might seem.

code.content:
import secrets

def generate_api_key(prefix="sk"):
    return f"{prefix}_{secrets.token_urlsafe(32)}"

key = generate_api_key()
print(key)  # sk_5f1e2c9a... long, unguessable

blocks.text: A recognizable prefix like sk for secret key is a small but genuinely useful convention, it lets automated scanners and even humans quickly spot a leaked key in a log file or a commit diff, which makes accidental exposure far easier to catch and react to quickly.
A short prefix like sk dash before the random portion also makes it easy for automated scanners, and human reviewers, to recognize a key at a glance.
3. Storing Keys on the Server Side

blocks.alt: Storing Keys on the Server Side
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440373676-655785028.png

A server should never store an API key in a way that lets anyone reading the database recover the original value, the same way passwords are never stored in plain text. The right approach is hashing the key with a strong one way function before saving it, and comparing an incoming request's key against that hash rather than a stored copy of the plaintext.

This means a database breach alone does not hand over usable credentials, an attacker who steals the hashes still cannot reconstruct the original keys, and can only make use of whatever specific keys they separately obtain in plaintext, such as through a live traffic capture.
A server should store only a hashed version of each key, similar to how passwords are stored, so that even a database leak does not directly expose usable keys.
Verifying an incoming key then becomes a matter of hashing the presented value and comparing it against the stored hash, exactly the same pattern used for password verification.
4. The One Time Reveal Pattern
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440373676-205273553.png

A common and sound pattern is showing a freshly generated API key to the user exactly once, at the moment it is created, and never displaying the full value again afterward. If the user loses it, the only recovery path is generating a brand new key, not retrieving the old one, which is a natural consequence of the server only ever storing a hash.

blocks.content: {"headers":["What is stored","What is shown"],"rows":[["Hash of the key","Never shown again"],["Key prefix, e.g. sk_5f1e","Shown in the dashboard for identification"],["Creation and last used timestamps","Shown in the dashboard"]]}

blocks.text: Keeping a short, non secret prefix visible in a dashboard is genuinely useful, it lets a user recognize which key is which across multiple integrations without the server ever needing to store or display the sensitive part again.

Showing a newly generated key exactly once, at creation time, and never again afterward, forces the caller to store it immediately and securely, rather than relying on the server to redisplay it later.
5. Scoping a Key to What It Actually Needs

blocks.alt: Scoping a Key to What It Actually Needs
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440373676-297845825.png

An API key should carry the same kind of least privilege thinking covered in the previous Authorization lesson, a key generated for a read only reporting integration should not also work for a tool that deletes records, even though it would technically be simpler to issue one universal key that does everything.

Letting a user create multiple, narrowly scoped keys for different integrations, rather than pushing everyone toward a single all powerful key, makes the eventual leak of any one of them far less damaging.
A key scoped only to read access cannot be misused to write or delete data even if it leaks, scoping narrowly is one of the cheapest, most effective defenses available.
6. Where a Key Belongs in a Request

An API key should travel in a request header, never in a URL query parameter. Query parameters have a habit of ending up in server access logs, browser history, and referrer headers sent to third party sites, all places a secret should never casually appear.

code.content:
# correct
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}
requests.get(url, headers=headers)

# avoid
requests.get(f"{url}?api_key={api_key}")  # leaks into logs

blocks.title: Headers, not query strings
blocks.content: A key placed in a URL tends to end up copied into logs and browser history far more often than one placed in a header.
{"headers":["Location","Recommended"],"rows":[["Authorization header","Yes"],["URL query parameter","No, easily logged or leaked"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Rotating Keys on a Schedule
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440373677-265321163.png

Because an API key has no natural expiry unless the server imposes one, rotation has to be a deliberate practice rather than something that happens automatically. A reasonable default is expiring keys after a fixed window, say ninety days, and prompting the owner to generate a replacement before the old one stops working.

code.content:
def is_expired(key_record):
    return now() > key_record["created_at"] + timedelta(days=90)

blocks.text: Supporting a brief overlap window, where both the old and new key work for a short grace period, makes rotation far less disruptive for an integration that cannot be updated instantly, and removes the temptation to simply never rotate a key because doing so would break something in production.

code.content:
# issuing a new key while briefly keeping the old one valid
new_key = generate_key()
old_key.set_expiry(days=7)   # grace period for callers to switch over

blocks.text: 8. Revoking a Key Immediately When It Leaks

blocks.alt: Revoking a Key Immediately When It Leaks
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440373677-63539758.png

A key that leaks, whether through a committed config file, a pasted support ticket, or a compromised laptop, needs a fast, reliable way to be shut off, ideally in seconds rather than waiting for a scheduled rotation. This means the verification check has to look at live state on every request, not a cached decision from earlier in the session.

Practicing this before it is needed matters, a team that has never actually revoked a key under pressure often discovers, during a real leak, that the revocation path was never fully wired up or was slower than expected.
Revocation should take effect immediately and be checked on every single request, not cached for any noticeable length of time, since every extra minute a leaked key stays valid is extra risk.
9. Never Hardcoding Keys in Source Code

An API key typed directly into a source file will, sooner or later, end up committed to version control, and version control history is extremely hard to fully scrub once a secret lands in it. Keys belong in environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager, a topic covered in full in the Secrets Management lesson later in this module.

code.content:
import os

api_key = os.environ["THIRD_PARTY_API_KEY"]  # never a literal string in the file

blocks.text: A useful habit is running an automated secret scanner as part of your commit process, catching an accidentally hardcoded key before it is pushed is dramatically cheaper than rotating it after the fact.

code.content:
# wrong: hardcoded directly in source
api_key = "sk-abc123"

# right: loaded from environment at runtime
import os
api_key = os.environ["API_KEY"]

blocks.text: 10. Detecting Leaked Keys in the Wild

Beyond preventing leaks, it helps to actively watch for signs that a key has already gotten out, unusual request volume from a single key, requests from geographies that make no sense for the owner, or a sudden spike in failed calls right before a successful one, which can indicate someone probing a stolen key's remaining scope.

items: A sudden spike in request volume from one key
Requests from an unexpected geography or IP range
Calls to tools that key has never used before
A burst of authorization failures followed by a success

blocks.text: Automated alerting on these signals turns a leaked key from a silent, ongoing problem into something a team notices and revokes within minutes rather than weeks.
Some teams scan public code repositories for accidentally committed key patterns, catching a leak within minutes rather than months.
11. Per Key Rate Limiting
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440373677-453295249.png

Rate limiting each API key individually, rather than the server as a whole, keeps one misbehaving or compromised key from being able to exhaust capacity that other legitimate keys depend on. It also gives you an early warning signal, a key suddenly hitting its rate limit is often the first visible sign that something about that key has changed, for better or worse.
12. Logging Key Usage Without Logging the Key

Every request authenticated by a key is worth recording, which key was used identified by its non secret prefix or a stored identifier, what it was used for, and when, but the raw key value itself should never appear in a log line. A logging pipeline that captures full request headers by default is a surprisingly common way for keys to leak.

blocks.title: Redact before you log
blocks.content: Configure logging middleware to strip or mask authorization headers by default, rather than trusting every future engineer to remember to do it by hand.

blocks.text: Logging which key ID made a request is useful for auditing, logging the actual key value itself defeats the purpose of keeping it secret in the first place.
13. When an API Key Is the Wrong Tool

API keys work well for server to server integrations and trusted automated clients, but they are a poor fit whenever a server needs to act on behalf of an individual human user against a third party service, especially one the user did not build. In that situation the delegated, revocable, scoped nature of OAuth, covered in the next lesson, is a much better match.

A simple test is asking whether the credential represents a person or a system. A key representing a backend service calling another backend service is usually fine, a key meant to represent a specific human's authority to act on a third party account is usually a sign OAuth is the more appropriate choice.
A scenario involving a specific human user acting through a third party service is usually better served by OAuth, covered in the next lesson, than by a shared, static API key.
Worked Example

A small analytics MCP server lets client applications query aggregated usage data. The team issues one API key per registered client, hashes it before storing, scopes each key to read only access, and shows the full key exactly once at creation time in the client's dashboard.

When one client's key later shows up in a public code sample by mistake, the team revokes it within minutes using the record's id, issues a fresh key, and updates the client's integration, all without needing to touch any other client's credentials, precisely because each key was scoped and stored independently from the start.
This same generation, storage, and rotation pattern applies whether the key is used for a single internal service or distributed to hundreds of external customers.
Common Mistakes

items: Generating keys from a predictable source instead of a cryptographically secure random generator
Storing keys in plaintext instead of a one way hash
Passing a key in a URL query parameter where it ends up in logs
Issuing one universal key instead of scoping keys to what each integration actually needs
Never rotating or expiring keys because nothing forces it
Logging full request headers, which silently captures raw keys

blocks.text: A further common mistake is issuing a single shared key used by every caller, making it impossible to revoke access for just one misbehaving client without affecting everyone else.
Practice

Build a small key issuing endpoint that generates a cryptographically random key, hashes it before storing, shows the raw value exactly once, and records a scope list alongside it. Then write a verification function that rejects requests with a missing, invalid, or revoked key, and a revocation function that takes effect on the very next request, not after any delay or cache expiry.
As a stretch, add per key rate limiting and a simple usage log that records which key was used and when, without ever writing the raw key value to that log.
Sketch what your revocation process would look like if a key was accidentally committed to a public repository, and how quickly it could be detected and rotated.
Key Takeaway

An API key is a simple, powerful tool precisely because it is just a string, and that simplicity demands discipline, generate it randomly, store only a hash, scope it narrowly, and be ready to revoke it the instant it leaks. Treat every key as something that will eventually be exposed, and design your storage and logging so that exposure is an inconvenience rather than a disaster.

API keys are a fine fit for trusted server to server integrations, but they fall short the moment a server needs to act on behalf of a specific human user against a third party service, which is exactly the gap the next lesson, OAuth, is built to close.
Treat every API key with the same seriousness as a password, generated randomly, stored hashed, scoped narrowly, and rotated on a predictable schedule.
